quizzes.stem: An assistant is asked to tally the letter r in a long part number and gives a wrong, confident figure. The team wants a fix that holds for every part number. Which approach is best?

options.a: Hand the counting to a small script and use its output
options.b: Add a system line demanding an exact character count every time
options.c: Move to a model with a larger context window available
options.d: Run the same question five times and take the most common figure

explanation.a: The model works on pieces, not letters, so a character-level tally is an approximation and a small program answers it exactly (the tokenizer section and the first trap).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "a model answers it by approximation", so a demand for exactness does not change how the part number is cut into pieces.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "The window is how much text fits per request", a capacity that does not change how a part number is cut into pieces.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Questions about individual characters (how many letters, which letter is third, reverse this string) are harder for it than they look", so repeating the question repeats the weakness.

quizzes.stem: A team corrects the assistant by hand after it repeats a mistake across many chats, and expects it to do better next week. They call the API directly. Which expectation is accurate?

options.a: The weights absorb the fix and apply it to every later session by default
options.b: A tuned copy of the model is created under the account for later calls
options.c: Only a request that carries the amended guidance in its own input gains from it
options.d: Requests to a model with a larger window gain from it whatever they carry

explanation.c:
Weights are fixed at inference and what looks like learning is the context window (the weights section),
   so only a call that carries the fix in its input can use it.
explanation.a:
Ruled out because "A conversation with Claude
   does not teach it anything that carries to the next conversation".
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "The Claude API does
   not currently offer fine-tuning", so no tuned copy is made by calling it.
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "The window is
   how much text fits per request", and a request holds only what is sent with it, so a larger window does not
   bring the fix into a call that leaves it out.

quizzes.stem: A stakeholder asks why a deployed assistant answers a question with an answer, when the raw model it started from tends to continue the question with more questions. Which part of how models are made does most to explain the gap?

options.a: Pretraining on a far larger corpus than the raw model saw
options.b: A later round of tuning on curated examples and replies ranked by people
options.c: A separate look-up store of answers that the assistant consults
options.d: A larger attention mechanism that lets the model reread the whole question

explanation.b: Fine-tuning and feedback training are the stages that turn a text continuer into an assistant (the stages section).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the stage list says of pretraining that "The result is capable and unruly", and a bigger corpus does not change that.
explanation.d: Ruled out because in attention "every position in the context can look at every earlier position", in the raw model as much as in the assistant.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "There is no third place such as a notebook it consults": everything the model uses is in the window or in the weights.

quizzes.stem: A company wants Claude to answer from its product manual, which is revised every month, through the Claude API. An engineer proposes fine-tuning on each new version. What is the best response?

options.a: Rely on what the model absorbed in training from earlier editions
options.b: Retrain the weights each month through a fine-tuning request to the API
options.c: Paste corrections into the chat and rely on the model to recall them later
options.d: Include the current edition in the context sent with each call

explanation.d: Knowledge that changes monthly belongs in the context, and the glossary says the Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning (the second trap and the table).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "the Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning", so the monthly request cannot be made through this route.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table lists "Memory of your previous conversations" among the things training does not give, so pasted corrections are not recalled.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the table lists "Knowledge of anything after the cut-off" among the things training does not give, and "the standard route is to put the knowledge in the context".

quizzes.stem: A research team trains a model for harmlessness the Constitutional AI way and wants it to handle one kind of request differently in the next run. In that method, what do people edit to steer that behaviour?

options.a: The written principles that both the critiques and the AI judge apply
options.b: The rankings that people give to pairs of answers for the preference model
options.c: The revised answers, corrected by hand before they become training data
options.d: The pretraining corpus, labelled by hand as harmful or harmless text

explanation.a:
In Constitutional AI "the only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles", so the
   principles are what people rewrite to change the behaviour (page 2, the Constitutional AI section).
explanation.b:
is ruled
   out because the preference model "is trained from this dataset of AI preferences", and for harmlessness "no human
   labels are needed for it".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "The model critiques its own answers against the principles
   and rewrites them", and those revisions become the training data without a hand edit.
explanation.d:
is ruled out because
   pretraining needs no labels: "Nobody labels the data; the text itself is the answer key."

quizzes.stem: A localisation lead budgets translation runs by word count, then finds that one paragraph needs noticeably more tokens in one language than in another. Which explanation fits best?

options.a: That language was added by later fine-tuning, which re-cut its text into extra pieces
options.b: The larger window used for that language forces the text into finer pieces
options.c: The learned vocabulary stores longer pieces for text that was common in the corpus
options.d: The translated text simply contains more words, and tokens track words one to one

explanation.c: The vocabulary was learned from a corpus, so a language that was common gets longer pieces and a rarer one splits into more (page 1, what the tokenizer does to your work).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the tokenizer is "built before pretraining and fixed afterwards", so later fine-tuning cannot re-cut any text.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "The window is how much text fits per request", and the trap on window and vocabulary says "They are unrelated settings", so the window does not set the piece size.
explanation.d: Ruled out because a token is not a word: "a Claude token is about 3.5 English characters", and "the exact number can vary depending on the language used".

quizzes.stem: A reviewer waves through a number in a report because the assistant is described as built to tell the truth. Which reply is the soundest?

options.a: Written principles removed unsupported claims, so a skim of the figure is enough
options.b: Recall can be fluent yet wrong, so trace the figure to its source before use
options.c: The model said it was sure of the figure, so its own second look is the control
options.d: A prompt can demand truthfulness, so add that line and skip the check

explanation.b: Facts sit in the weights as tendencies, "which is why recall can be wrong in a fluent way" (page 1), and the glossary calls HHH "a research framework that informs how Claude is trained", not a certificate on a reply, so the figure is traced to its source before it goes in the report.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the table lists "A guarantee that any statement is true" among the things training does not give.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the table sets "Tendencies toward honest, harmless replies" against "A rule that can never be broken", so a line asking for truthfulness only restates a tendency and the figure still needs a check.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Verification is still the user's job", so the model saying it is sure, and looking again, does not replace a check against the source.

quizzes.stem: A team is automating four chores. Which one should be done by a deterministic program instead of the model alone?

options.a: Sorting yesterday's incoming emails by urgency from the message text
options.b: Rewriting this week's release notes for a non-technical customer audience
options.c: Proposing likely causes for last night's intermittent failing test
options.d: Pulling yesterday's order count from the company database

explanation.d: The table lists "Access to your files, systems or today's date" among the things training does not give, so a figure held in a company system has to be fetched by code (page 2, the table).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Following instructions and a helpful manner", which covers rewording notes for a reader.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Reasoning patterns it can apply to new problems", which covers proposing causes.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Fluent language, many languages, code", and judging urgency from message text is language work.
